authors: James Bessen
title: Accounting for Rising Corporate Profits: Intangibles or Regulatory Rents?
venue: Boston University School of Law, Law and Economics Research Paper No. 16-18 (SSRN working paper)
method: Firm-level decomposition of Tobin's Q and operating margins on R&D, organisational capital, lobbying, campaign spending and RegData regulation counts; difference-in-differences around major regulatory changes against matched control firms
finding: Capital investment and R&D explain much of the rise in valuations and profits in the 1990s, but political activity and regulation account for a surprisingly large share since 2000; firms experiencing major regulatory change see valuations rise about 12% relative to matched controls.
summary_plain: US company profits have risen since 1980. This study finds that since 2000 much of the rise is linked to regulation and lobbying, not only to innovation: firms hit by big new rules tended to become more valuable, not less.
relevance: Regulation can create rents for incumbents who can absorb compliance costs, so heavy EU digital rulebooks may entrench large platforms as well as constrain them.
caveats: US-only working paper, never published in a peer-reviewed journal; regulation counts are a crude proxy, and the DiD covers a limited set of major regulatory events.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: European Commission, Directorate-General for Competition (with OECD and Lear-led background studies)
title: Protecting competition in a changing world - Evidence on the evolution of competition in the EU during the past 25 years
venue: European Commission staff report (DG COMP), Publications Office of the EU, KD-09-24-494-EN-N
method: Descriptive industry-level CR4 concentration (Orbis) and firm-level markups (production-function approach), market-level sales data, plus OECD regressions linking concentration and markups to upstream regulatory burden and a macro model (MATER) simulation of markup effects on GDP
finding: Average firm markups across 23 European countries and 204 industries rose by 7% between 2000 and 2019, and average industry CR4 concentration rose by about 5 percentage points; a model simulation attributes a GDP loss of about 5.7% to the 7.54% markup increase if it fully reflects weaker competition. OECD regressions find industries relying on inputs from more heavily regulated sectors show higher concentration, but the report says the evidence is not sufficient to conclude with high certainty that rising regulatory barriers drove the trend.
summary_plain: The Commission's own review finds that competition in the EU has weakened over 25 years: big firms hold larger shares and charge higher margins. It says rules that raise the cost of doing business may help larger firms, but the evidence is not yet conclusive.
relevance: It is the Commission's own evidence base. It names regulatory barriers to entry as a possible cause of rising market power, and it cites the DMA as an example of pro-competitive regulation.
caveats: Mostly descriptive. Markup estimates depend on production-function assumptions, and the GDP figure is a model simulation that assumes the whole markup rise reflects lost competition.
interested_party: DG COMP is the EU competition enforcer and argues for stronger competition policy
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: George J. Stigler
title: The Theory of Economic Regulation
venue: The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2(1): 3-21
geography_period: US (illustrative evidence on trucking weight limits and occupational licensing)
method: Political-economy theory of the supply and demand for regulation, with illustrative cross-state evidence
finding: As a rule, regulation is acquired by the industry and is designed and operated primarily for its benefit; concentrated producer interests outbid dispersed consumers for entry control, subsidies and price-fixing.
summary_plain: This classic paper argues that industries often seek regulation and shape it to protect themselves from competition. It is the origin of the idea of 'regulatory capture'.
relevance: It is the basic theory behind the worry that complex EU digital rules can be shaped by, and end up favouring, the large incumbents they are meant to discipline.
caveats: A theory with mostly illustrative evidence. Later work (Peltzman, Becker) shows that regulators also weigh consumer interests.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Anne O. Krueger
title: The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society
method: Theoretical model of competitive rent-seeking for import licences, with back-of-envelope estimates of rent values
finding: Rents created by government restrictions were estimated at about 7.3% of national income in India (1964), and import-licence rents alone at about 15% of GNP in Turkey (1968); competition for these rents wastes resources beyond the usual deadweight loss.
summary_plain: When governments hand out valuable permissions, firms spend real resources competing for them instead of producing. Krueger coined the term 'rent-seeking' and showed these rents can be large.
relevance: Licensing, designation and compliance regimes create valuable regulatory positions, and the effort spent lobbying for them is a cost of regulation in its own right.
caveats: Context is trade licensing in developing economies; the rent estimates are rough, and Krueger did not estimate how much of the rents were dissipated.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Jan De Loecker; Jan Eeckhout; Gabriel Unger
title: The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications
method: Firm-level markups estimated with the production-function approach (output elasticity over cost share) from Compustat accounts
finding: Aggregate markups rose from 21% above marginal cost in 1980 to 61% by 2016, driven by the upper tail while the median is unchanged; the average profit rate rose from 1% to 8%.
summary_plain: Using company accounts, the authors find that US firms charge much higher prices relative to their costs than they did in 1980. The rise comes mostly from a small group of top firms.
relevance: This is the main benchmark for the 'rising market power' debate that EU digital competition policy, including the DMA, responds to.
caveats: Markup levels depend on the production-function assumptions and on treating overhead as a variable cost, and listed firms are not representative; others estimate smaller increases.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Germán Gutiérrez; Thomas Philippon
title: How European Markets Became Free: A Study of Institutional Drift (NBER WP 24700 revision titled 'How EU Markets Became More Competitive Than US Markets')
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 21(1): 251-292 (NBER Working Paper 24700, 2018)
method: Political-economy model of national vs supranational regulators, tested with cross-country data on concentration, profits, product-market regulation and competition-authority independence
finding: European markets now have lower concentration, lower excess profits and lower regulatory barriers to entry than US markets; EU institutions are more independent and enforce competition more strongly than any individual country ever did, and countries with weaker institutions benefit most from delegation to the EU level.
summary_plain: Since the 1990s Europe's markets have become more open and competitive than America's. The authors credit independent EU-level competition enforcement and the deregulation of formerly protected sectors.
relevance: It suggests EU-level rules and enforcers can push against capture and incumbency, which is the main counterweight to the regulatory-rents view.
caveats: Evidence is largely cross-country and descriptive. Later revisions focus on telecoms and airlines, and the EC 2024 report finds EU concentration rising after 2000.
themes: market power and regulatory rents
productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Germán Gutiérrez; Thomas Philippon
title: The Failure of Free Entry
method: Industry panel of entry rates on Tobin's Q; tests rival explanations (returns to scale, technology) against RegData regulation and lobbying expenditure, with an instrument-based analysis of regulation's effect by firm size
finding: The elasticity of entry with respect to Tobin's Q was positive and significant until the late 1990s but fell to zero afterwards; lobbying and regulations, not returns to scale or technology, explain the decline, and regulations reduce entry and growth of small firms relative to large ones, particularly in high-lobbying industries.
summary_plain: Profitable US industries used to attract new competitors, but since about 2000 they no longer do. The authors blame growing regulation and lobbying, which hurt small and new firms more than big ones.
relevance: It supports the view that regulation weighs most on small firms, which matters for the cumulative compliance load of EU digital law on start-ups and SMEs.
caveats: Working paper; US-only; regulation measured by RegData word counts. Goldschlag and Tabarrok find no link between regulation and declining dynamism.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Thomas Philippon
title: The Great Reversal: How America Gave Up on Free Markets
venue: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press (book)
method: Book-length synthesis of the author's and others' research on concentration, profits, prices, lobbying and regulation
finding: US industries have become more concentrated and less competitive than European ones since the late 1990s, with higher prices (for example in mobile telecoms and airlines), lower investment and productivity; the author attributes this to lobbying and campaign finance that raised entry barriers and weakened antitrust.
summary_plain: Philippon argues that the US, once the model of free markets, now has less competition than Europe, and that lobbying by big firms is a main reason.
relevance: It is often cited for the claim that EU competition institutions have done better than US ones, and it frames lobbying-driven regulation as a risk.
caveats: Written for a general audience, so it argues a case; some claims (for example on prices and welfare) are disputed by other economists.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Matias Covarrubias; Germán Gutiérrez; Thomas Philippon
title: From Good to Bad Concentration? US Industries over the Past 30 Years
method: Industry-level relationships among concentration, prices, investment, intangibles and leader productivity, split by period and initial concentration
finding: In the 1990s concentration was efficient, driven by tougher price competition, intangible investment and leaders' productivity; after 2000 it became inefficient, associated with lower investment, higher prices, lower productivity growth and rising barriers to entry.
summary_plain: Market concentration is not always bad. In the 1990s it reflected better firms winning; after 2000 it increasingly reflected entrenched leaders protected by barriers.
relevance: It warns against reading concentration in digital markets as automatically harmful or benign, and it points to barriers to entry (including regulatory ones) as the distinguishing factor.
caveats: Correlational industry evidence; classifying concentration as good or bad depends on proxies.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Gábor Koltay; Szabolcs Lőrincz; Tommaso Valletti
title: Concentration and Competition: Evidence From Europe and Implications For Policy
method: Industry concentration (CR4, HHI) built from Orbis and Euromonitor data, plus aggregate profitability from national accounts
finding: Average industry concentration rose moderately over two decades, with a considerably larger share of high-concentration industries, a tendency toward oligopoly, and a sustained rise in aggregate profitability.
summary_plain: In Europe too, more industries are now dominated by a few large firms, and profits have risen, though less sharply than in the US.
relevance: It is Europe-specific evidence that market power is growing, and it feeds directly into the EC 2024 report and the case for ex-ante digital rules.
caveats: Descriptive; does not identify whether regulation or technology drives the trend; concentration measured at industry, not antitrust-market, level.
interested_party: Authors are (or were) DG COMP economists; Valletti is a former DG COMP Chief Economist
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Shikhar Singla
title: Regulatory Costs and Market Power
method: Machine learning on regulatory documents to measure industry compliance costs; panel regressions of firm outcomes on regulatory-cost shocks by firm size
finding: Regulatory costs rose by $1 trillion over 1970-2018; higher regulatory costs lower sales, employment, markups and profitability for small firms and raise them for large firms, and increased regulation can explain 31-37% of the rise in market power.
summary_plain: Compliance costs fall harder on small companies than big ones. This study estimates that growing US regulation explains about a third of the increase in big firms' market power since 1970.
relevance: It is direct evidence that compliance burdens can raise concentration, a key risk when many EU digital instruments apply to firms of all sizes.
caveats: Unpublished working paper; the cost measure comes from ML classification of regulatory text; US-only.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Dustin Chambers; Patrick A. McLaughlin; Tyler Richards
title: Regulation, entrepreneurship, and firm size
geography_period: US industries (RegData 3.0 linked to Census SUSB data), late 1990s-2010s
method: Industry panel regressions of firm counts and employment by firm size on RegData industry-specific regulatory restriction counts, with industry and year fixed effects
finding: A 10% increase in industry-specific regulatory restrictions is associated with a 0.5% reduction in the number of firms and a 0.6% reduction in employment only among small firms; consecutive years of high regulatory growth amplify the negative effects for small firms but not large ones.
summary_plain: More rules in an industry go with fewer firms and fewer jobs at small businesses, while large firms are largely unaffected.
relevance: It uses restriction counts, the same kind of measure as this site's counts of legal restrictions, and links them to small-firm outcomes.
caveats: Associational; restriction word counts do not measure stringency; the 2018 working paper said only small-firm counts fell.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), a market-oriented think tank that built RegData
themes: market power and regulatory rents
firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Sara Calligaris; Chiara Criscuolo; Luca Marcolin
title: Mark-ups in the digital era
venue: OECD Science, Technology and Industry Working Papers, No. 2018/10
method: Firm-level markups estimated by the production-function approach on Orbis data, compared across sectors by digital intensity
finding: Average markups rose (about 8% over 2001-2014, as summarised in the EC 2024 report), driven by firms at the top of the distribution; digital-intensive sectors have higher markups than other sectors and the gap widened over time.
summary_plain: Across rich countries, firms' price margins rose in the 2000s, and the rise was greatest in sectors that use digital technology intensively.
relevance: It ties rising market power to digital-intensive sectors, the target of the DMA and related EU instruments.
caveats: Descriptive; the markup level depends on estimation assumptions; the 2024 update finds product-market regulation does not explain the digital markup gap.
themes: market power and regulatory rents

authors: Nathan Goldschlag; Alexander Tabarrok
title: Is regulation to blame for the decline in American entrepreneurship?
method: Industry panel linking Census business-dynamism measures (startup rates, job reallocation) to RegData federal regulation counts
finding: Rising federal regulation does not explain the long-run decline in US startup rates and job reallocation; the decline is broad-based across industries regardless of their regulatory growth.
summary_plain: This study finds no clear link between the growth of US federal rules and the long-run fall in new business creation.
relevance: It is contrary evidence: counts of regulation alone may not predict harm to entry, so cumulative-burden claims about EU digital law need careful testing.
caveats: RegData counts may miss stringency and uncertainty; covers federal rules only (not state licensing).
interested_party: Tabarrok is affiliated with the Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which built RegData
themes: market power and regulatory rents
firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Luis Garicano, Claire Lelarge, John Van Reenen
title: Firm Size Distortions and the Productivity Distribution: Evidence from France
method: Structural Lucas span-of-control model estimated from bunching of the firm size distribution just below the 50-employee threshold where labour laws bind
finding: The 50-employee rules are equivalent to a 2.3% variable tax on labour; with French real-wage rigidity welfare costs are 3.4% of GDP (1.3% if wages were fully flexible). Workers and large firms lose, small firms gain.
summary_plain: French firms pile up just below 50 employees, where many labour rules start to apply. The authors estimate these rules cost the economy about 3.4% of GDP, mostly at the expense of workers.
relevance: EU digital laws also use size thresholds (e.g. DSA VLOP 45m users, DMA gatekeeper criteria, SME carve-outs), which can create similar bunching and growth disincentives.
caveats: Result depends on the structural model and wage-rigidity assumption; concerns labour law, not digital regulation.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud, John Van Reenen
title: The Impact of Regulation on Innovation
method: Endogenous growth model with size-contingent regulation; discontinuity in innovation at the 50-employee threshold plus responses to exogenous export-demand shocks
finding: The share of innovating firms falls sharply just below the 50-employee threshold and their innovation response to demand shocks is muted; regulation reduces aggregate innovation by 5.7% (AER abstract; the 2021 NBER version reported 5.4% and a 2.2% consumption-equivalent welfare loss).
summary_plain: Firms close to a regulatory size threshold innovate less, because growing would bring extra rules. Across France this lowers overall innovation by around 6%.
relevance: Shows that size-based regulatory burdens can depress innovation, the core output EU digital policy aims to protect.
caveats: Effects mainly on incremental innovation; the NBER version finds regulated firms that do innovate pursue more radical breakthroughs.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Simeon Djankov, Rafael La Porta, Florencio Lopez-de-Silanes, Andrei Shleifer
title: The Regulation of Entry
method: New cross-country dataset on procedures, time and official cost to start a business; cross-country correlations
finding: Official entry costs are extremely high in most countries; heavier entry regulation is associated with more corruption and larger unofficial economies but not better public or private goods quality.
summary_plain: Counting the steps, days and fees needed to open a company in 85 countries, the authors find that heavy start-up rules go with more corruption and a bigger informal economy, not better products or services.
relevance: Founding paper of the World Bank Doing Business approach and of counting rules as a measure of regulatory burden, the method this site applies to EU digital law.
caveats: Correlational; measures formal rules on paper, not enforcement or benefits.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Leora Klapper, Luc Laeven, Raghuram Rajan
title: Entry Regulation as a Barrier to Entrepreneurship
geography_period: Western and Eastern Europe, late 1990s (Amadeus firm data)
method: Difference-in-differences across industries: entry in naturally high-entry industries (US benchmark) compared across countries with different entry costs
finding: Costly entry regulations reduce creation of new firms, especially in naturally high-entry industries, force entrants to be larger, and slow growth of incumbents in those industries.
summary_plain: In European countries where starting a company is expensive, fewer new firms appear in sectors that would naturally see many start-ups, and those that do enter start bigger.
relevance: European evidence that fixed regulatory costs filter out small entrants, a key concern for digital markets with many start-ups.
caveats: Cross-sectional identification; US industry entry rates as benchmark may not reflect 'natural' entry everywhere.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Marianne Bertrand, Francis Kramarz
title: Does Entry Regulation Hinder Job Creation? Evidence from the French Retail Industry
method: Regional and time variation in zoning-board approvals of large stores, instrumented by the political composition of the boards
finding: Approval requirements created entry barriers that weakened retail employment growth; retail employment could have been more than 10% higher without the regulation.
summary_plain: France required local boards to approve big new shops. Where boards blocked more stores, fewer retail jobs were created; without the rule there might be over 10% more retail jobs.
relevance: Classic evidence that ex-ante approval regimes protecting incumbents cost jobs, relevant to authorisation and gatekeeping-style rules.
caveats: Single sector and country; IV relies on board politics affecting jobs only through approvals.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Francesco Trebbi, Miao Ben Zhang
title: The Cost of Regulatory Compliance in the United States
method: Establishment-level occupation data combined with occupation task content to estimate wage bill spent on compliance; IV to separate requirements from enforcement
finding: Compliance labour costs average 1.34% of a firm's wage bill, rising over time; the share follows an inverted U by size, peaking around 500 employees.
summary_plain: US firms spend on average about 1.3% of their payroll on staff whose work is complying with rules. Mid-sized firms bear the highest share, not the smallest or largest.
relevance: Gives a measured order of magnitude for compliance costs and suggests burdens fall hardest on mid-sized 'scale-ups', where EU digital firms often struggle.
caveats: Counts only labour compliance costs, not capital, external advisers or forgone activity; working paper.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Joseph Kalmenovitz
title: Regulatory Intensity and Firm-Specific Exposure
geography_period: United States, listed firms (federal paperwork regulations)
method: Firm-specific regulatory intensity built from administrative paperwork-burden data and machine learning; panel regressions with heterogeneity by financial constraints
finding: Higher regulatory intensity raises costs of goods sold and overhead, and leads firms to cut capital investment, hire fewer employees and lobby more, especially when financially constrained.
summary_plain: Firms facing more federal paperwork rules spend more on overheads, invest and hire less, and lobby more, particularly firms short of cash.
relevance: Firm-level evidence on the channels (cost, uncertainty, lobbying) through which regulatory volume affects investment and jobs.
caveats: Paperwork burden is a partial measure of regulation; listed US firms only.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: James B. Bailey, Diana W. Thomas
title: Regulating Away Competition: The Effect of Regulation on Entrepreneurship and Employment
method: Industry fixed-effects regressions of firm births and employment (Statistics of US Businesses) on RegData regulation counts
finding: More-regulated industries had fewer new firm births and slower employment growth; large firms were less likely than small firms to exit heavily regulated industries.
summary_plain: US industries with more federal rules saw fewer new businesses and slower job growth, and big firms coped with the rules better than small ones.
relevance: Supports the concern that rule volume raises entry barriers and favours incumbents, a central argument in debates on digital regulation.
caveats: Fixed-effects correlations; magnitudes not reported in abstract; contrasts with Goldschlag & Tabarrok using similar data.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which builds RegData and advocates regulatory reform
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Bentley Coffey, Patrick A. McLaughlin, Pietro Peretto
title: The Cumulative Cost of Regulations
method: Multisector Schumpeterian endogenous-growth model whose closed-form solution gives the estimating equation, fitted with RegData 2.2
finding: Regulation has dampened US growth by about 0.8 percentage points per year since 1980; the economy would have been roughly 25% larger in 2012 had regulation stayed at 1980 levels.
summary_plain: By adding up the small yearly drag of accumulating rules, this study estimates the US economy would be about a quarter bigger if federal regulation had stayed at its 1980 level.
relevance: The most-cited estimate of the cumulative macro cost of regulatory accumulation, often invoked in debates about the stock of EU rules.
caveats: Costs only, no benefits measured; large counterfactual extrapolation from model structure.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which builds RegData and advocates regulatory reform
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: John W. Dawson, John J. Seater
title: Federal Regulation and Aggregate Economic Growth
method: Time-series measure of federal regulation (pages of the Code of Federal Regulations) in an endogenous growth framework
finding: Regulation has caused substantial reductions in the growth rates of US output and TFP and offers an explanation for the 1970s productivity slowdown (authors' abstract; no single figure verified here).
summary_plain: Using the page count of US federal rules over half a century, the authors conclude that regulation significantly slowed economic and productivity growth.
relevance: Early macro evidence linking the volume of regulatory text to growth, the logic behind counting restrictions in EU law.
caveats: Aggregate time series with few observations; page counts are a coarse proxy; widely debated magnitudes.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Miriam Bruhn
title: License to Sell: The Effect of Business Registration Reform on Entrepreneurial Activity in Mexico
method: Difference-in-differences using staggered municipal rollout of a business-registration simplification
finding: Simplifying entry raised registered businesses by 5% and wage employment by 2.2%, while lowering incumbents' income by 3%; informal firms did not register more.
summary_plain: When Mexican towns made it easier to register a business, more people (mainly former employees) opened firms and employment rose, though existing businesses earned somewhat less.
relevance: Quasi-experimental evidence that cutting administrative entry burdens raises entry and jobs, but with modest effects and no formalisation gain.
caveats: Developing-country context; effects modest; only registration procedures, not substantive rules.
interested_party: Author at the World Bank, which promotes business-registration reform
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: European Commission, DG Enterprise and Industry (Expert Group)
title: Models to Reduce the Disproportionate Regulatory Burden on SMEs: Report of the Expert Group
method: Expert group review of national evidence and good practices on SME regulatory burden
finding: Where a big enterprise spends one euro per employee to comply with a regulatory duty, a medium-sized enterprise might spend around four euros and a small business up to ten euros.
summary_plain: The Commission's experts estimated that, per worker, small firms can pay up to ten times more than large firms to comply with the same rule.
relevance: The source of the EU's 'Think Small First' and SME-test logic, which shapes proportionality and SME exemptions in digital legislation.
caveats: Indicative estimate drawn from earlier studies, not a new causal analysis; dated.
themes: firms: size, entry, compliance costs and jobs

authors: Philippe Aghion, Nick Bloom, Richard Blundell, Rachel Griffith, Peter Howitt
title: Competition and Innovation: An Inverted-U Relationship
geography_period: UK firms (patents at the US patent office)
method: Schumpeterian growth model plus panel estimates of patenting on product-market competition (Lerner index) (identification draws on policy-driven changes in competition)
finding: Model and data both show an inverted-U: innovation rises with competition at low levels and falls at high levels; the inverted-U is steeper in 'neck-and-neck' industries where firms are technologically close.
summary_plain: More competition boosts innovation up to a point, after which it can dampen it. Whether a rule that increases competition helps innovation depends on how competitive the market already is.
relevance: The DMA's premise is that gatekeeper markets sit on the low-competition side of the curve, where opening them up should raise innovation.
caveats: Core evidence from UK manufacturing patents; later replications find the shape sensitive to specification.
themes: innovation

authors: Knut Blind
title: The influence of regulations on innovation: A quantitative assessment for OECD countries
method: Country panel regressions of innovation indicators on economic, social and institutional regulation indices (OECD taxonomy), within an endogenous-growth framework
finding: Effects depend on the type of regulation and differ between short and long run; general legal framework quality, efficient IP regimes, unrestricted price setting, product/service legislation and environmental laws are associated with more innovation.
summary_plain: Regulation is not one thing: some kinds of rules go with more innovation and others with less. Clear legal frameworks and product rules can help innovation, while heavy-handed economic controls tend to hurt it.
relevance: Supports judging EU digital instruments by type and design rather than by the overall number of rules.
caveats: Small country panel, correlational; survey-based regulation indices.
themes: innovation

authors: Stefan Ambec, Mark A. Cohen, Stewart Elgie, Paul Lanoie
title: The Porter Hypothesis at 20: Can Environmental Regulation Enhance Innovation and Competitiveness?
venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy 7(1): 2-22
method: Review of theory and empirical tests of the Porter hypothesis (Porter and van der Linde 1995, JEP 9(4)) and its 'weak', 'narrow' and 'strong' versions
finding: Evidence that well-designed (especially flexible, market-based) regulation spurs innovation (weak version) is fairly strong; evidence that it raises overall firm competitiveness (strong version) remains mixed.
summary_plain: The idea that smart regulation can push firms to innovate and even become more competitive has some support. Rules often trigger new inventions, but whether firms end up better off overall is less clear.
relevance: The main theoretical argument for regulation-induced innovation, often invoked for EU digital rules (e.g. privacy-enhancing technologies).
caveats: Evidence base is environmental, not digital; transfer to data and platform rules is by analogy.
themes: innovation

authors: Ariel Dora Stern
title: Innovation under regulatory uncertainty: Evidence from medical technology
geography_period: US FDA high-risk medical device approvals (multi-decade sample)
method: Comparison of approval times for pioneer vs follow-on entrants within device categories, and before/after publication of FDA guidance documents
finding: Pioneer device entrants spend 34% (7.2 months) longer in regulatory approval than follow-on entrants, a cost upwards of 7% of bringing a new high-risk device to market; delays reflect regulatory uncertainty, and fall when objective guidance is published.
summary_plain: First movers pay a price when the rules are unclear: the earliest new medical devices took months longer to approve. Clear official guidance cut those delays.
relevance: New EU digital rules (DMA, AI Act) create similar uncertainty for first movers; guidance and specification decisions can lower it.
caveats: Medical devices, US; magnitudes not directly transferable to digital markets.
themes: innovation

authors: Anu Bradford
title: The False Choice Between Digital Regulation and Innovation
method: Legal and institutional analysis (law review article), no new econometrics
finding: Argues the US-EU tech gap is not explained by strict EU digital regulation but by deeper factors: fragmented digital single market, shallow capital markets, punitive bankruptcy law, risk-averse culture, and weaker ability to attract global talent.
summary_plain: Europe's lag in tech is mostly not caused by its digital rules. Missing venture capital, a fragmented market and harsh failure laws matter more.
relevance: The leading counter-argument to claims that EU digital rules explain Europe's innovation gap.
caveats: Argumentative synthesis, not causal estimation; author is a prominent scholar of EU regulatory influence.
themes: innovation

authors: Jian Jia, Ginger Zhe Jin, Liad Wagman
title: The Short-Run Effects of the General Data Protection Regulation on Technology Venture Investment
geography_period: EU vs US and rest of world tech ventures, 2014-2019
method: Difference-in-differences around GDPR enforcement (May 2018), EU ventures vs US/rest-of-world ventures, Crunchbase and VentureXpert data
finding: Negative post-GDPR effects on EU ventures in the number of deals, total dollars raised and dollars per deal; the INFORMS release reports a 26.1% reduction in monthly deals for EU ventures relative to US ventures in the first year.
summary_plain: After GDPR, European tech start-ups raised less venture money and closed fewer deals than comparable US start-ups. The study only covers the first year.
relevance: Direct evidence that a major EU digital regulation can reduce early-stage investment in European tech.
caveats: Short window (under one year post); confounding with other 2018 EU-US shocks hard to rule out.
themes: innovation

authors: Avi Goldfarb, Catherine E. Tucker
title: Privacy Regulation and Online Advertising
geography_period: EU vs non-EU countries, 2000s (around the ePrivacy Directive)
method: Difference-in-differences on randomized ad-exposure field tests (3.3 million respondents, 9,596 campaigns) around the EU ePrivacy Directive
finding: After the EU privacy laws, display ads became far less effective at changing stated purchase intent relative to other countries, an average reduction of about 65%, concentrated on general-content sites and plain banner ads.
summary_plain: Once EU rules limited tracking, online ads in Europe became much less effective. That hits the revenue model of free websites such as news sites.
relevance: Early causal evidence that EU data rules shift economics of ad-funded digital services, a mechanism also relevant for DMA data-combination limits.
caveats: Outcome is stated purchase intent, not sales; pre-GDPR regime.
themes: innovation

authors: Garrett A. Johnson
title: Economic Research on Privacy Regulation: Lessons from the GDPR and Beyond
method: Survey of the empirical economics literature on the GDPR
finding: The literature has largely, though not universally, documented harms to firms (performance, innovation, competition, the web, marketing), alongside some objective privacy improvements; identification is hard because of weak control groups, uneven compliance and changed data observability.
summary_plain: Most studies find GDPR imposed costs on businesses, but some show real privacy gains. Measuring the benefits is much harder than measuring the costs.
relevance: The best single overview of how a flagship EU digital regulation affected firms and innovation.
caveats: Working paper; consumer-benefit side under-measured by construction.
themes: innovation

authors: Garrett A. Johnson, Scott K. Shriver, Samuel G. Goldberg
title: Privacy and Market Concentration: Intended and Unintended Consequences of the GDPR
method: Panel event study of website vendor use for EU vs non-EU users around GDPR enforcement
finding: The week after enforcement, website use of web technology vendors fell 15% for EU residents and vendor-market concentration rose 17%, with Google and Facebook vendors gaining relative share; aggregate changes dissipated by end-2018 but persisted in advertising.
summary_plain: GDPR cut websites' use of data vendors but helped the biggest players, Google and Facebook, gain share. Privacy rules can unintentionally strengthen dominant firms.
relevance: Shows how compliance costs can entrench gatekeepers, a tension the DMA aims to correct.
caveats: Mostly short-run; effects faded for aggregate measures.
interested_party: Acknowledges funding from the Marketing Science Institute and the George Mason University Program on Economics & Privacy (which has received tech-industry funding)
themes: innovation

authors: Christian Peukert, Stefan Bechtold, Michail Batikas, Tobias Kretschmer
title: Regulatory Spillovers and Data Governance: Evidence from the GDPR
method: Difference-in-differences on third-party HTTP requests, 12 months before and 6 months after GDPR, comparing sites by exposure to EU law
finding: Websites substantially reduced interactions with web technology vendors, including sites not legally bound by GDPR, especially less popular sites; all vendors lost, but Google lost relatively less and gained market share in advertising and analytics.
summary_plain: GDPR changed how websites worldwide use data, even outside Europe. Smaller vendors lost out while Google gained ground.
relevance: Evidence of the 'Brussels effect' and of concentration side-effects from EU digital rules.
caveats: Measures data flows, not welfare or innovation directly.
themes: innovation

authors: Carl Benedikt Frey, Giorgio Presidente (earlier working-paper version with Chinchih Chen)
title: Privacy regulation and firm performance: Estimating the GDPR effect globally
geography_period: Global firms with varying EU exposure, around 2018
method: Difference-in-differences by firm exposure to EU markets with firm and country-industry-year fixed effects
finding: GDPR lowered the profitability of firms targeting European consumers through a cost channel: technology firms saw a 2.1% decline in profits but not in sales; GDPR raised extra expenses and wage bills, accelerated patenting in GDPR-related fields, and burdens fell mainly on smaller firms.
summary_plain: GDPR raised costs and cut profits for firms selling to Europeans, hitting smaller companies hardest. It also spurred new privacy-related inventions.
relevance: Quantifies compliance costs and their uneven incidence by firm size, while also showing regulation-induced innovation.
caveats: Exposure-based design; profit effects modest and heterogeneous; earlier WP figures differ from published abstract.
themes: innovation

authors: Rebecca Janssen, Reinhold Kesler, Michael E. Kummer, Joel Waldfogel
title: GDPR and the Lost Generation of Innovative Apps
method: Event study of app exit and entry around GDPR plus a structural model of demand and entry for counterfactual equilibria
finding: GDPR induced the exit of about a third of available apps and halved new app entry in the following quarters; in the long-run counterfactual GDPR reduces consumer surplus and aggregate app usage by about a third.
summary_plain: After GDPR, many apps disappeared and far fewer new ones launched. The authors estimate users lost a lot of value from the missing apps.
relevance: Among the largest estimated innovation costs of an EU digital regulation, relevant to cumulative compliance burdens on small developers.
caveats: Global app store with no clean non-GDPR control; welfare relies on structural assumptions; privacy benefits not valued.
themes: innovation

authors: Colleen Cunningham, Florian Ederer, Song Ma
title: Killer Acquisitions
method: Theory plus difference-in-differences comparing development of acquired drug projects that overlap vs do not overlap with acquirer's portfolio
finding: Acquired projects are less likely to be developed when they overlap with the acquirer's portfolio, especially where the acquirer has market power; conservatively 5.3%-7.4% of acquisitions in the sample are killer acquisitions.
summary_plain: Some big firms buy up start-ups to shut down rival products. Weak competition oversight can therefore cost innovation.
relevance: Underpins DMA Article 14 merger-notification duties for gatekeepers: lax regulation can also harm innovation.
caveats: Pharma, not digital; mechanism in tech is debated.
themes: innovation

authors: Sai Krishna Kamepalli, Raghuram Rajan, Luigi Zingales
title: Kill Zone
method: Theoretical model of platform competition, app developer adoption and VC financing under expected acquisition
finding: The prospect of quick acquisition by an incumbent platform reduces app developers' incentive to adopt an entrant, lowering the entrant's stand-alone value and acquisition price, and so reducing VC incentives to fund entry: a 'kill zone' around incumbents.
summary_plain: When start-ups expect to be bought by a tech giant, fewer users and partners back them and investors fund fewer of them. Unchecked platform power can choke off innovation.
relevance: Theoretical case that ex-ante platform regulation such as the DMA could raise start-up investment rather than reduce it.
caveats: Theory; empirical support for kill zones is limited and contested.
themes: innovation

authors: Giuseppe Nicoletti; Stefano Scarpetta
title: Regulation, productivity and growth: OECD evidence
venue: Economic Policy 18(36): 9-72 (also OECD ECO WP 347; World Bank PRWP 2944)
method: Industry-level panel regressions of multifactor productivity growth on OECD product market regulation and privatisation indicators, with a catch-up-to-frontier specification
finding: Reforms promoting competition and private governance are associated with faster productivity growth; in manufacturing, liberalisation gains are larger the further a country is from the technology leader, suggesting entry-limiting regulation slows technology adoption. Strict product market regulation and lack of reform appear to underlie the weak productivity of some continental European countries.
summary_plain: Countries that lowered barriers to entering markets saw faster productivity growth, especially where they had most catching up to do. Heavily regulated European economies lagged.
relevance: Seminal source for the claim that rules restricting entry and competition widen the EU-US productivity gap; the DMA aims to raise contestability, but other digital rules may raise entry costs.
caveats: Aggregate regulation indices; associations from panel data with limited exogenous variation; pre-digital era.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Renaud Bourlès; Gilbert Cette; Jimmy Lopez; Jacques Mairesse; Giuseppe Nicoletti
title: Do Product Market Regulations in Upstream Sectors Curb Productivity Growth? Panel Data Evidence for OECD Countries
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 95(5): 1750-1768 (NBER WP 16520)
method: Endogenous-growth model tested on an industry panel; MFP growth regressed on regulation in supplier (upstream) sectors weighted by input-output links, interacted with distance to frontier
finding: Anticompetitive upstream regulations significantly curbed MFP growth over the preceding fifteen years, more strongly for observations close to the productivity frontier.
summary_plain: When the sectors that supply other businesses (such as telecoms, transport or professional services) are tightly regulated, productivity suffers downstream too, especially for the most advanced firms.
relevance: Digital platforms and cloud/network services are upstream inputs for much of the economy, so the costs or benefits of regulating them spill over to user industries.
caveats: Regulation measured with OECD indices; identification relies on input-output weights and frontier interactions rather than a natural experiment.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Jens Arnold; Giuseppe Nicoletti; Stefano Scarpetta
title: Regulation, Allocative Efficiency and Productivity in OECD Countries: Industry and Firm-Level Evidence
venue: OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 616
geography_period: OECD countries, harmonised firm-level data, c. 1990s-2000s
method: Industry allocative-efficiency (Olley-Pakes covariance) comparisons and firm-level productivity regressions interacting service regulation with ICT-use intensity and distance to frontier
finding: Resources were allocated less efficiently across firms where service regulation was less market-friendly; anti-competitive service regulation hampered productivity growth in ICT-using sectors, especially for firms catching up to or near the technology frontier.
summary_plain: Tight rules in service sectors made it harder for the best firms to grow and take resources from weaker ones, which slowed productivity in industries that rely on digital technology.
relevance: Directly links regulation to slower ICT-driven productivity in continental Europe, the channel most relevant to digital regulation.
caveats: Working paper; regulation indices are pre-2008 and not specific to digital rules.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Alberto Alesina; Silvia Ardagna; Giuseppe Nicoletti; Fabio Schiantarelli
title: Regulation and Investment
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 3(4): 791-825 (NBER WP 9560)
geography_period: OECD countries, transport, communications and utilities sectors, 1975-1998
method: Sector-country panel regressions of investment on time-varying OECD regulation indicators (entry barriers, public ownership), with fixed effects and GMM
finding: Various measures of product market regulation, particularly entry barriers, are robustly and negatively related to investment; reforms that liberalise entry are very likely to spur investment.
summary_plain: Sectors where it is harder for new firms to enter invest less; opening them up tends to raise investment.
relevance: Investment in digital infrastructure and AI is central to the EU-US gap; rules that act as entry barriers may depress it, while rules opening gatekept markets may raise it.
caveats: Network industries only; regulation indices coarse; endogeneity of reforms addressed only partly.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Olivier Blanchard; Francesco Giavazzi
title: Macroeconomic Effects of Regulation and Deregulation in Goods and Labor Markets
method: General-equilibrium model with monopolistic competition in goods markets and wage bargaining in labour markets; regulation sets entry costs, competition and worker bargaining power
finding: Deregulation reduces and redistributes rents; even if beneficial in the long run, it can bring incumbent decline, temporarily higher unemployment and lower real wages. Product market deregulation can make labour market deregulation politically easier.
summary_plain: Cutting red tape can raise output and jobs over time, but the gains take time and create winners and losers along the way.
relevance: Frames why regulatory reform in the EU is politically hard and why short-run and long-run effects of digital rules can differ.
caveats: Theoretical; no direct estimate of magnitudes.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Bart van Ark; Mary O'Mahony; Marcel P. Timmer
title: The Productivity Gap between Europe and the United States: Trends and Causes
method: Growth accounting with EU KLEMS industry data decomposing labour productivity into ICT capital, other capital, labour quality and MFP
finding: Since the mid-1990s US labour productivity growth accelerated while Europe's slowed; the gap reflects slower emergence of the knowledge economy in Europe (lower ICT investment contributions, a small ICT-producing sector and slower MFP growth), concentrated in market services, with labour market functioning and high product market regulation as underlying issues.
summary_plain: Europe fell behind the US from the mid-1990s mainly because it used digital technology less productively, especially in services such as retail and finance.
relevance: Establishes that the EU-US gap is largely a digital and services story, the arena of EU digital regulation.
caveats: Accounting decomposition, not causal; regulation named as an underlying factor rather than estimated.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Nicholas Bloom; Raffaella Sadun; John Van Reenen
title: Americans Do IT Better: US Multinationals and the Productivity Miracle
method: Compares US-owned, other multinational and domestic establishments operating under the same European regulations; event study of takeovers by US vs non-US multinationals; links to management practices survey
finding: US multinationals in Europe obtained higher productivity from IT than non-US multinationals, and establishments taken over by US multinationals (but not others) raised the productivity of their IT; the US IT-related productivity advantage is primarily due to tougher 'people management' practices.
summary_plain: American-owned firms in Europe get more out of computers than European firms facing the same rules, mainly because of how they manage people.
relevance: Important counterweight: part of the EU-US digital gap reflects management and organisation rather than regulation per se (though labour rules can shape management practices).
caveats: Mostly UK data; management practices can themselves be shaped by labour regulation.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Dan Andrews; Chiara Criscuolo; Peter N. Gal
title: The Best versus the Rest: The Global Productivity Slowdown, Divergence across Firms and the Role of Public Policy
method: Tracks productivity of global frontier vs laggard firms; regressions of the frontier-laggard gap on sectoral product market reform intensity
finding: Labour productivity at the global frontier grew 2.8% a year in manufacturing in 2001-2013 versus 0.6% for non-frontier firms, with an even wider gap in market services; divergence was stronger in industries where product market reforms were least extensive.
summary_plain: The most productive firms keep pulling ahead while the rest stall, and the gap is widest where markets are less open to competition.
relevance: Digital regulation can help (by opening markets to challengers) or hurt (by raising fixed compliance costs for laggards) technology diffusion.
caveats: Working paper; reform-divergence link is correlational; frontier measures sensitive to Orbis coverage.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Mario Draghi (for the European Commission)
title: The future of European competitiveness (Part A: A competitiveness strategy for Europe)
method: Policy diagnosis drawing on macro comparisons, sector studies and stakeholder input
finding: Real disposable income per capita has grown almost twice as much in the US as in the EU since 2000; around 70% of the per capita GDP gap with the US at PPP (which rose from 31% in 2002 to 34%) is explained by lower productivity. The EU has around 100 tech-focused laws and over 270 regulators active in digital networks, and many EU laws take a precautionary ex ante approach that the report says hampers innovation.
summary_plain: The EU's former central bank chief found Europe falling behind the US mainly on productivity and argued that layers of tech regulation and a fragmented single market hold innovators back.
relevance: The most influential recent EU diagnosis directly naming the volume of digital regulation as a drag on innovation.
caveats: Policy report, not peer-reviewed; the 100-laws count is an inventory, not an impact estimate.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Isabel Schnabel (ECB Executive Board)
title: From laggard to leader? Closing the euro area's technology gap
venue: ECB speech, European University Institute, Florence, 16 February 2024
method: Speech synthesising ECB staff and academic research
finding: Big-four euro area labour productivity rose from 25% of the US level in 1945 to 100% in 1995, then fell back to about 0.8 by 2008; US services productivity grew 3.2% a year in 1995-2005 versus 0.9% in Europe. She cites evidence that strict product market regulation, rigid labour markets and red tape inhibited digital adoption, and that intra-EU services trade is only about 15% of GDP versus over 50% for goods because of remaining regulatory barriers.
summary_plain: A senior ECB official argued that Europe's productivity gap with the US is largely about slow adoption of digital technology, held back by red tape, fragmented markets and weak scale-up finance.
relevance: Central-bank view that fragmentation and entry barriers, rather than regulation as such, are the main issue, favouring harmonised single-market rules.
caveats: Speech; numbers drawn from cited studies, not original estimates. In a February 2026 speech ('Made in Europe') she called the 'over-regulation' narrative misleading while stressing internal barriers and national gold-plating.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: International Monetary Fund, European Department (underlying work: Adilbish, Cerdeiro, Duval, Hong, Mazzone, Rotunno, IMF WP 2025/040)
title: Regional Economic Outlook: Europe, October 2024 (and 'Europe's Productivity Weakness: Firm-Level Roots and Remedies', IMF WP/25/40)
venue: IMF Regional Economic Outlook; IMF Working Paper
geography_period: EU vs US states, trade costs for 2020; firm data Europe and US
method: Structural gravity model comparing cross-border with domestic trade flows; residual trade costs converted to ad valorem tariff equivalents
finding: Intra-EU trade costs in 2020 were equivalent to an ad valorem tariff of about 44% for the average manufacturing sector (vs about 15% between US states) and about 110% for services. The working paper finds smaller markets and limited market-based finance are key bottlenecks for Europe's frontier firms.
summary_plain: The IMF estimates that hidden barriers inside the EU's single market, such as differing national rules, raise costs as much as a large tariff would, especially for services.
relevance: Supports the case that EU-level harmonised digital rules can replace 27 national regimes and reduce internal trade costs.
caveats: Residual-based gravity estimate captures all border frictions (language, distance, preferences), not only regulation; critics (e.g. a VoxEU column, Bini Smaghi at Bocconi IEP) argue it is too high and sensitive to data choices; some sources quote 45%.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: European Parliamentary Research Service (Joseph Dunne et al.)
title: Europe's two trillion euro dividend: Mapping the Cost of Non-Europe, 2019-24
method: Compilation of sectoral 'cost of non-Europe' estimates of gains from adopting and implementing Parliament-backed EU policies
finding: Potential gains of over EUR 2.2 trillion (about 14% of 2017 EU GDP) if Parliament-backed policies were adopted and fully implemented over 2019-2029, measured mainly as additional GDP.
summary_plain: The European Parliament's research service estimates that completing pending EU-level policies, including the digital single market, could add very large sums to EU output over a decade.
relevance: Common source for the claim that more (harmonised) EU regulation raises GDP, the opposite of the burden narrative.
caveats: Aggregates heterogeneous studies with different methods; produced by an institution that advocates EU action; gains are cumulative over ten years, not annual.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap

authors: Thierry Mayer; Vincent Vicard; Soledad Zignago
title: The cost of non-Europe, revisited
geography_period: EU member states, gravity data to the 2010s
method: Structural gravity estimation of EU single market trade creation versus ordinary regional trade agreements, then general-equilibrium counterfactuals (shallow RTA or WTO rules, with/without Brexit)
finding: Working-paper version: the Single Market raises bilateral trade more than three times as much as a typical regional trade agreement, and the trade-related cost of non-Europe is about 3% to 7% of GDP on average depending on the counterfactual, largest for small open (especially Eastern) economies.
summary_plain: Deep EU integration, including common rules, has boosted trade among members far more than ordinary trade deals, and undoing it would cost several percent of GDP.
relevance: Evidence that harmonised rules (as opposed to national ones) raise trade and income, relevant to the single-market rationale of EU digital laws.
caveats: Headline numbers confirmed in the working paper, not checked in the journal text; captures all EU integration, not regulation alone.
themes: productivity, GDP and the EU-US gap
